kicker: splat-walk, a phone that never was

scenes.headline: How a splat scan becomes phone footage
scenes.sub: A simulated walker, head and phone over a Gaussian splat
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Saunter! This looks like phone footage of a London passage. It is a Gaussian splat, and the person filming is simulated too.

scenes.text: Model the person and the phone, not the camera path: a gait, a head on springs, and a shutter that reads each row at its own instant.
scenes.mark: reads each row at its own instant
scenes.say: The idea: do not fly a camera along a spline. Simulate the person holding it, and a sensor that reads each row at its own instant.

scenes.title: Three layers of motion
scenes.say: The pose is built in layers, each a function of time.

items.say: First the walk. Cadence rises with speed, and the head bobs about four centimetres a step.
Then the head. It chases each thing it looks at like a damped spring, and bigger turns take longer.
Then the phone, chasing the head through a stiffer spring. That is the camera that renders.

scenes.title: One frame of the film pass

steps.say: Each video frame, the splats are drawn once, from the pose at the frame's own time.
The walk is asked again, just before and just after, to cover the exposure and the readout.
For every pixel, the film pass moves the ray to where the phone was at that row's instant, and averages ten taps.
Top rows come out earlier than bottom rows, so a turning phone leans every vertical edge.

scenes.title: Shear at the biggest head turn
scenes.say: At the biggest head turn, the formula predicts thirty two point five pixels of lean. My re-run of the shader loop measured thirty point nine.

steps.say: The exposure alone widens each edge into a soft band.
The readout alone slants it. The app does both.

scenes.text: The splats are drawn once a frame; the footage comes from moving each pixel's ray through its own slice of time.

recap: A gait, a head and a phone
Each a spring or a law of time
scenes.say: To recap: a gait, a head and a phone in layers, and a shutter that reads each row at its own moment.
